About the Simulation

This simulation visualizes bound states in a finite quantum potential well, demonstrating how discrete energy levels emerge from mathematical constraints. The potential matches the lecture notes: V = 0 outside the well and V = −V₀ for |x| < a; bound-state energies E are quoted with zero at infinity (so E < 0).

The constant ℏ²/(2m) is set to a pedagogical value (not the SI free-electron value) so that typical well depths and widths produce a clear number of bound states in this demo.

Bound-state energies are fixed by the intersection of a transcendental curve with a circle in the (k, η) plane:

Here k is the wave number inside the well, η is related to decay outside the well, and a is the half-width. Each intersection corresponds to an allowed energy.

N is the number of bound states for the currently selected parity (even or odd). Adjust V₀ to see states appear/disappear as the circle expands/contracts. Finite wells support only a finite number of bound states.

Potential and wavefunctions
η(k) vs k plot

Guided Inquiry

1 · The finite well

Here’s the setup. A particle moves in a well of depth V₀ and half-width a: the potential is 0 outside and −V₀ for |x| < a. A bound state is one with −V₀ < E < 0 — it’s trapped, unable to reach infinity.

2 · The classical particle

Let’s start with the classical picture. Imagine a classical particle trapped in this well. Which energies between −V₀ and 0 do you think it can have?

3 · A shallower well

Right now, three even-parity levels fit this well. Let’s make it shallower: the depth is about to be cut to its smallest value, V₀ = 1 eV, with the half-width unchanged. How many even-parity bound states do you think will be left?

4 · Squeezing the well

Now push it as far as it goes. The half-width is about to be cut to a = 0.1 nm as well — the weakest well this apparatus can make. What do you think becomes of that last even state?

5 · Filling the well

One last experiment — let’s fill the well back up. The half-width returns to a = 0.5 nm, and V₀ is then raised from 1 eV upward. How do you think the collection of bound states will grow?

The Physics

The finite square well · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A particle in a finite well has a wave that oscillates inside the well and extends past its walls. This sim builds that wave for a well of depth V₀ and half-width a, and shows what the energies, the tails and the number of bound states depend on.

What you'll learn

  • How the wave inside the well joins the wave outside, and what that demands of the energy.
  • How to read a bound state's energy E and its tail length δ off the η–k panel.
  • How far the wave reaches past the walls, and what sets that distance.
  • How the number of bound states depends on V₀ and a, through a single number z₀.
The well: V = 0 outside, −V₀ for |x| < a. The orange curve sketches a wave of the kind the sim draws at an energy E.

What's on screen

  • Grey step (left plot): the potential V(x). The blue-tinted region is the well, between the dashed lines at x = ±a.
  • Coloured curves: each state's ψ, drawn on its own level line (E0, E1, …) across the well.
  • η–k plot (right): the matching curve (orange even, violet odd) and the blue circle. Each crossing is a dot in its state's colour.
  • Bound States panel: N, and each state's E (eV) and δ (nm).
See itSwitch the sim to the odd family, with the same well. Watch for: the orange curve in the η–k plot replaced by a violet one, and the wavefunctions on the left changing shape.

Fixed: ħ²/2m = 0.0381 eV·nm² (the free-electron value). V = 0 outside the well and −V₀ inside, so every bound energy is negative.

03

A bound wave dies away outside

Take an energy E between −V₀ and 0, with zero at infinity. The wave has a different form in each region:

k and η are real and positive. For odd states the outside wave changes sign across x = 0.
  • Inside, E is above V, so ψ oscillates.
  • Outside, E is below V. The equation allows e−η|x| and e+η|x|, and only the decaying one can be normalised, ∫|ψ|² dx = 1.
  • At x = ±a the inside wave must join the outside wave smoothly. At most energies the join also needs the growing exponential, so there is no bound state there.
The sim's defaults, V₀ = 10 eV and a = 0.5 nm, using the sim's own construction of ψ. Left: E = −2.86 eV, an allowed energy. Right: E = −3.50 eV, which is not.

Nothing discrete is imposed by hand: requiring a normalisable wave selects the energies.

See itThe sim hides its curves for an instant, then draws them again. Watch for: every curve returning on one of its own level lines, E0, E1, …, and nowhere else.
04

Matching at the walls picks the energies

Requiring ψ and its slope to be continuous at x = a leaves one condition on k and η:

The matching condition for the even and odd families.

The two are not independent, because both come from the same E:

A circle in (ka, ηa), radius z₀.
  • The η–k plot draws both: the matching curve and the circle. Its axes are k and η in nm⁻¹, so the circle's radius is z₀/a = √(V₀/0.0381) nm⁻¹, which is 16.2 nm⁻¹ at the defaults.
  • Each crossing of curve and circle is one bound state. The sim numbers them 0, 1, 2, …
  • z₀ = a√(V₀/0.0381), with a in nm and V₀ in eV, is 8.10 at the defaults. Only V₀ and a enter it.
See itSame well, other family: the curve changes and the circle does not. Watch for: the blue circle staying the same size while the violet −cot branches cross it at new places.
05

Reading energy and tail from a crossing

A crossing gives a pair (k, η), and both the energy and the tail length follow from it:

The Bound States panel prints E in eV and δ in nm for each crossing.
V₀ a

These sliders move the sim too.

  • Zero is set at infinity, so every bound energy is negative, and −V₀ is the floor of the well.
  • N in the panel counts one family at a time. The line above counts both.
  • The tail length δ = 1/η = ħ/√(2m|E|) is how far the wave extends past a wall before it has fallen to 1/e of its value there.
See itRun your current well through the sim. Watch for: a level line on the plot for each E in the Bound States panel, with the panel's N counting the even states.
06

The wave reaches past the walls

The wave in the region |x| > a.
  • Past a wall ψ is small but not zero, so the probability density |ψ|² is not zero where V is greater than E. A classical particle there would need negative kinetic energy. The wave itself needs no trajectory, so none is implied.
  • The reach δ = 1/η is set by |E|, how far E sits below zero. A state near E = 0 reaches furthest. At the defaults the lowest even state has δ = 0.06 nm, and the least-bound odd state has δ = 0.41 nm.
  • The density |ψ|² is a probability per unit length. The probability of finding the particle outside is the area under it there.
See itShow |ψ|² in place of Re(ψ). Watch for: each curve rising above its own level line past the dashed wall lines, instead of stopping at them.
07

How many states a well holds

Each time z₀ passes a multiple of π/2, the circle reaches one more branch of the matching curves, and one more state appears. The two families take turns:

Counts for each family, and in total (⌈ ⌉ means round up).
  • The even curve starts at the origin, so any circle crosses it. A one-dimensional well always binds at least one state.
  • States arrive one at a time, alternating even, odd, even, … Never in pairs.
  • Only z₀ sets the count. At a = 0.5 nm the whole V₀ slider gives 2 to 10 states in total.
The count against V₀ at a = 0.5 nm. The marked point is the opening well.
See itThe weakest well the sim can make, V₀ = 1 eV and a = 0.1 nm. Watch for: N = 1, with one level near the top of the well and a wave extending far past the walls.
See itTwo different wells with the same z₀ = 7.25, run one after the other. Watch for: the same N both times, with every energy changed.
08

Where it matters

  • Quantum-well lasers. A layer a few nanometres thick, between layers of a wider-gap semiconductor, confines electrons in a finite well. Its thickness helps set the energy levels, and so the colour of the light. In GaAs the electron's effective mass is about 0.067 mₑ, so ħ²/2m is about 15 times the sim's value and the same well holds fewer levels.
  • The deuteron. The neutron–proton well is a three-dimensional well of a similar kind. It holds a single bound state about 2.2 MeV below threshold. The scales are MeV and femtometres, not eV and nanometres.
  • Tunnelling. The tail e−η|x| is the same wave behaviour that carries a particle through a thin barrier. A scanning tunnelling microscope's current changes steeply with the gap for this reason.
Go deeper: the weakest well
The shallow-limit estimate, to first order in z₀².
  • For z₀ ≪ 1 the one state sits just below E = 0 and its tail is long, δ = 1/η ≈ a/z₀².
  • The estimate is rough where z₀ is not small. At V₀ = 1 eV and a = 0.1 nm, z₀ = 0.51: it gives 0.26 eV, and the sim's solver gives 0.196 eV.
09

Summary

In one line. A finite well binds the energies at which the wave inside joins a decaying tail outside. The number z₀ = a√(V₀/0.0381) sets how many there are.

Key points

  • Bound states have −V₀ < E < 0: ψ oscillates inside and decays outside.
  • A crossing of the matching curve with the circle k² + η² = V₀/0.0381 gives k, η, E and δ = 1/η.
  • |ψ|² is not zero past the walls, out to about δ.
  • States appear one at a time as z₀ grows by π/2. A one-dimensional well always has one.

Common mix-ups

  • "N = 3 means the well has three states." N counts one family. The defaults have 3 even and 3 odd.
  • "A shallow enough well binds nothing." In one dimension it always binds one. The weakest well here has one, at E = −0.196 eV.
  • "E < 0 means below the floor of the well." Zero is at infinity. The floor is −V₀.

Things to try on your own

  • Set V₀ = 8 eV, a = 0.5 nm, then V₀ = 32 eV, a = 0.25 nm. Compare N and the energies for both families.
  • At a = 0.5 nm, raise V₀ from 1 eV until a second even state appears. The exact threshold is z₀ = π, V₀ = 1.504 eV.
  • At the defaults, show |ψ|² and compare the tails of E0 and E2 with their δ values.
